text.p: Sterling rallied to a 20-month high in early trading, cracking 2.40 marks for the first time since February 1995, as buoyant UK bond and stock markets got caught in the slipstream of the dash for convergence trades in Europe.
Although off early record peaks, the FTSE 1000 share index held above the freshly captured 4,000 level during the session, while gilt futures set new contract highs.

Chartists said the break of 2.3960 marks late Wednesday was bullish, as that was a 50 percent retracement of the entire 1994-1995 fall. Traders said options were triggered just under 2.40 in early trade and a big U.S. hedge fund was also involved.
"The European convergence story is so dominant at the moment that people are determined to drag the UK into the equation," said Michael Burke, economist at Citibank in London.
"The fact of the matter is that, given the way Spain, Italy and Sweden have been performing recently, UK real yields are now very attractive on a comparative basis."
Analysts dismissed scattered rumours about future UK plans for re-entry to the European exchange rate mechanism as premature and unthinkable ahead of a UK general election.
At 0950 GMT, the pound was trading at 2.3985/90 marks compared with 2.3930/35 late in Europe on Wednesday.
Against the dollar, the pound was at $1.5650/60 compared with $1.5670/77 in Europe late Wednesday.

The pound has risen 3.9 percent against the mark and 2.1 percent on a trade-weighted basis in just over a month as robust UK monetary and economic activity indicators have thrown cold water on the prospects of another pre-election UK base rate cut.

A chronic background concern for sterling, that brisk growth will suck in imports and balloon the current account deficit, has also been assuaged since better-than-expected second-quarter current account data were released last month.
Recent UK reserves data, meantime, has puzzled analysts.
Reserves have been falling steadily in recent months, with September underlying reserves down another $113 million.
Given the recent strength of the pound, analysts would have expected the opposite.

Some analysts suggest that the Treasury's effective veto of the Bank of England's request for a base rate rise may have led the central bank to encourage sterling gains as a way of tightening monetary conditions by other means.
Either way, the policy response to sterling's appreciation will now be crucial to the direction of the currency.
